newsitem.title: USA: Ford in talks for Detroit stadium name rights.
newsitem.headline: Ford in talks for Detroit stadium name rights.

text.p: Ford Motor Co Chairman Alex Trotman said Thursday the automaker was in talks with the Detroit Lions on a multi-million dollar deal to purchase naming rights to the football team's proposed new stadium.

Trotman, speaking to reporters following a Ford board of directors meeting at the automaker's world headquarters in Dearborn, said he expected the negotiations to be complete within the next several days.
He said reports that Ford would pay $30 million to $40 million for the naming rights "aren't far off" from the deal Ford was discussing with the National Football League team.
Trotman said the company wanted to have exclusive naming rights but has not yet decided on a specific name.
"It would be big-time Ford something -- we don't know what -- either Ford Stadium or Ford Dome," Trotman said.

Ford board members William Clay Ford and his son, finance committee chairman William Clay Ford Jr., who are owners of the Lions, abstained from discussions of the deal during Thursday's board meeting.
Edsel Ford II, another Ford family member on the board who has no interest in the franchise, did participate in the talks.
"We see it as a very important marketing opportunity for the company," Trotman said.

A contribution of $30 million to $40 million would help the $225 million domed stadium proposed for downtown Detroit clear a major financing hurdle. The Lions face a November 1 deadline to gain commitments for $50 million in corporate and private contributions.

Other components of the proposed financing package include a $50 million contribution from the Lions and an $80 million bond issue backed by new Wayne County taxes on hotel rooms and car rentals, which are subject to a referendum on the November 5 ballot.
The package also includes $20 million from the sale of surplus Wayne County land, and up to $45 million in bonds sold by the city of Detroit and the Detroit Downtown Development Authority.
The proposed 65,000-seat football stadium would be built at the end of the decade next to a new $240 million, open-air ballpark for the Detroit Tigers on the edge of downtown Detroit.

After the stadium's construction, the Lions would leave the Pontiac Silverdome in suburban Pontiac, Mich., where they have played for the past 21 years. The team has pledged to honor terms of their current lease, which expires in 2004.
The 80,000-seat Silverdome, opened in 1975 at a city-financed cost of $50 million, would become the youngest major league sports facility in the United States to be replaced with a new venue.
